title: Room and Well
premise: Jonah Ishikawa, a hospice nurse who documents the backwards-counting of the dying, moves to the village of Hollowmere to care for Edith Vane, whose final count ends at zero on the night a bell that was melted down in 1911 rings from the ruined church. The ringing marks everyone who took part in what the village buried in 1974—the drowning of a child, Ruth Callow, whose death was ruled an accident and whose family's land was quietly absorbed by her neighbors. Jonah discovers their own late mother's name in the ledger of witnesses and realizes they inherited not just her house but her debt. To survive, Jonah must return what was taken: exhume the truth, give Ruth back her name and her ground, and stand before the village as the bell counts down to its last toll. The book ends with Jonah surrendering the house and their own carefully kept records to the flooded well where Ruth lies, choosing witness over safety as the bell finally falls silent.
about_author: Mara Underhill is the pen name of a former hospice volunteer who spent six years sitting with the dying in rural England and never once heard them count. She writes horror about paperwork, inheritance, and the things families agree not to say out loud.

chapters.title: The Counting Ward
chapters.summary: Jonah Ishikawa introduces their habit of recording dying patients' backwards counts in a leather notebook, believing documentation is a form of prayer. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: tender compulsion—care as control, grief made orderly.

chapters.title: Hollowmere
chapters.summary: Jonah arrives at the village to nurse Edith Vane, inheriting use of their late mother's cottage. The villagers are polite but watchful; no one meets their eyes at the pub. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: unease beneath welcome, the sense of being measured.

chapters.title: Edith Counts to Zero
chapters.summary: Edith's backwards count accelerates over three nights, ending at zero exactly when every dog in Hollowmere howls. Her last words name a child: 'Ruthie's still under.' POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: dread crystallizing into obligation.

chapters.title: A Bell That Wasn't
chapters.summary: At Edith's funeral, the ruined church bell—one melted down in 1911 per the parish record Jonah finds—rings once across the valley. Only Jonah and a boy, Sam Petch, seem to hear it clearly. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: reality tilting; the past refusing burial.

chapters.title: The Ledger
chapters.summary: Sorting Edith's papers, Jonah finds a 1974 parish ledger listing witnesses to an 'incident at the well,' including their own mother's signature. The well on the old Callow property was capped that same year. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: inheritance curdling into guilt.

chapters.title: What the Neighbors Kept
chapters.summary: Jonah interviews elderly villager Harold Finch, who nearly speaks, then begs them to leave it buried: 'We paid already. We all paid.' His hands shake around a photograph of two children. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: the cost of collective silence.

chapters.title: Sam Hears It Too
chapters.summary: Twelve-year-old Sam Petch tells Jonah he hears the bell counting down—forty-one rings left—and that his grandfather warns him never to go near the Callow well. POV: alternating Jonah and Sam. Emotional beat: lonely children finding each other across generations.

chapters.title: Mother's House, Mother's Debt
chapters.summary: Jonah searches the cottage and finds their mother's hidden letters confessing she watched something happen at the well in 1974 and said nothing, trading silence for the Vane land lease. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: betrayal and recognition—the parent they mourned was complicit.

chapters.title: Thirty Rings
chapters.summary: The bell rings nightly now, audible to half the village. Livestock die; the well water turns sweet and cold. The parish council holds an emergency meeting Jonah is barred from. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: a community fracturing under a debt coming due.

chapters.title: The Drowned Girl's File
chapters.summary: In county archives Jonah finds Ruth Callow's file: drowned 1974, ruled accidental, body never recovered because 'the well was searched and cleared'—by men named in the ledger. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: cold fury; justice deferred for fifty years.

chapters.title: Harold Confesses
chapters.summary: Harold, hearing his own count begin, tells Jonah the truth: the village boys dared Ruth onto the well cover; it gave way; they hid the body rather than face blame, and their fathers sealed the well with her inside. POV: Harold, framed by Jonah. Emotional beat: confession as agony, too late to save him—he dies mid-sentence, counting.

chapters.title: The Village Turns
chapters.summary: Word spreads that Jonah is digging. Windows darken, tires slash, a note reads LEAVE THE WELL SEALED. Jonah realizes staying invisible was never an option—they were always going to be made the outsider or the scapegoat. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: isolation hardening into resolve.

chapters.title: Twenty Rings
chapters.summary: Sam goes missing overnight; he's found at the wellhead, sleepwalking, fingers bloodied from prying the cap. His mother blames Jonah and calls the police. POV: Sam, then Jonah. Emotional beat: terror that the debt may be collected from the innocent.

chapters.title: The Council's Bargain
chapters.summary: Parish council chair Gwen Ashcroft offers Jonah money and their mother's deeds signed over free—if they leave and let the village 'handle Ruth properly,' meaning another quiet erasure. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: temptation of complicity, refused.

chapters.title: Records Are Prayers
chapters.summary: Jonah compiles everything—ledger, letters, archive files, recordings of the counts—into a single document and mails copies to a journalist and a solicitor, so the truth will exist even if they don't. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: documentation transformed from coping into weapon and testament.

chapters.title: Fifteen Rings, Then Ten
chapters.summary: The bell's countdown accelerates. The well begins to ring too—a wet, metallic echo answering the bell. Villagers gather at night without agreeing to, drawn like tide. POV: multiple brief POVs. Emotional beat: communal dread becoming involuntary pilgrimage.

chapters.title: Gwen Breaks
chapters.summary: Gwen Ashcroft, whose father led the cover-up, confronts Jonah with a shotgun, then collapses into weeping: she has heard Ruth's voice in her taps for fifty years. She gives Jonah the original cap-stone key her father kept. POV: Gwen. Emotional beat: the enforcer of silence becoming its first defector.

chapters.title: Opening the Well
chapters.summary: Jonah, Sam, and Gwen unseal the cap at dawn as the village watches in frozen silence. Below, in the flooded dark, something small waits patiently, having counted longer than any of them. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: awe and horror braided—the dead kept faith better than the living.

chapters.title: Three Rings
chapters.summary: They cannot recover a body after fifty years underwater; instead Jonah performs a different restitution—reading Ruth's full name, date, and the true record of her death aloud to the assembled village, entering it into the parish register in ink. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: justice outside the law, spoken plainly; grief finally witnessed.

chapters.title: The Last Toll
chapters.summary: The bell rings three times, then once, then hangs silent forever. The well's water stills. But the ledger opens to a new page bearing one line: WHAT WAS TAKEN IN 1974 IS NOT YET ALL RETURNED. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: relief shadowed by the final price.

chapters.title: Room and Well
chapters.summary: Jonah understands: the house itself was bought with Ruth's silence, and the land must go back. They sign the cottage and grounds over to a memorial trust in Ruth Callow's name, keeping only the notebook. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: surrender as survival—the price paid willingly at last.

chapters.title: What I Heard at the End
chapters.summary: Epilogue: Jonah, working hospice again in a distant town, records one last entry—a dying stranger counting backwards who reaches one and says, softly, 'Thank you.' The notebook closes. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: peace earned, vigilance kept, prayer answered.
